identity.title: Medication review for edema: dihydropyridine CCB, NSAIDs, thiazolidinediones, pregabalin/gabapentin, steroids, minoxidil/hydralazine

technique.how: Review the list for agents started or up-titrated in the weeks before swelling: dihydropyridine CCBs (amlodipine, nifedipine), NSAIDs/COX-2 inhibitors, thiazolidinediones, pregabalin/gabapentin, corticosteroids, minoxidil/hydralazine, oestrogens, dopamine agonists. Ask dose, timing relative to onset, and whether swelling is bilateral, dependent and painless.
technique.prerequisites: Accurate medication list including OTC NSAIDs; baseline renal function and any history of heart failure.

interpretation.positive_finding: Bilateral, dependent, non-tender ankle edema beginning weeks after a dihydropyridine CCB, NSAID, thiazolidinedione, gabapentinoid or vasodilator supports drug-induced edema; NSAIDs with ACEi/ARB or diuretics additionally raise AKI and sodium retention.
interpretation.negative_finding: No culprit drug makes medication effect unlikely and shifts attention to heart failure, venous insufficiency, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome or hypoalbuminaemia.
interpretation.pitfalls: CCB edema is not diuretic-responsive and is often misdiagnosed as heart failure; thiazolidinediones and NSAIDs can precipitate true heart failure decompensation, so the presence of a drug does not exclude cardiac cause; unilateral or painful swelling is never 'drug edema'.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: stop/switch the agent (or add ACEi/ARB for CCB edema) and reassess in 2-4 weeks before echocardiography; negative: proceed with HF/venous/renal/hepatic workup.

sources.citation: Makani H, Bangalore S, Romero J, Htyte N, Berrios RS, Makwana H, Messerli FH. Peripheral edema associated with calcium channel blockers: incidence and withdrawal rate--a meta-analysis of randomized trials. J Hypertens 2011;29:1270-1280.
Heidenreich PA, Bozkurt B, Aguilar D, Allen LA, Byun JJ, Colvin MM, Deswal A, Drazner MH, et al. 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure. Circulation 2022;145:e895-e1032.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Unilateral, painful or acute-onset swelling; edema with dyspnoea, orthopnoea, elevated JVP or weight gain >2 kg - evaluate for DVT or heart failure regardless of medication history.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Thiazolidinedione or NSAID use with new edema plus dyspnoea may be drug-precipitated heart failure; NSAIDs with ACEi/ARB and diuretic ('triple whammy') with rising creatinine is AKI until proven otherwise.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: No accuracy or agreement data; attribution rests on temporal relation and resolution after withdrawal.

extraction_notes: No diagnostic-accuracy study evaluates medication history as a test for drug-induced versus other edema; evidence is incidence data from RCT meta-analysis and guideline cautions. Makani 2011 (PMID 21558959, Abstract): 'The weighted incidence of peripheral edema was significantly higher in the CCBs group when compared with controls/placebo (10.7 vs. 3.2%, P < 0.0001)'; incidence 'reaching 24 and 5%, respectively, after 6 months'; 'Incidence of peripheral edema in patients on DHPs was 12.3% compared with 3.1% with non-DHPs'; high-dose vs low-dose CCB 16.1 vs 5.7%. These are adverse-event incidences in hypertension trials, not sensitivity/specificity, so no estimate entered. AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 HF guideline (PMID 35363499) cautions against thiazolidinediones and NSAIDs in HF (guideline text; unverified recall of section). No study found for gabapentinoid, steroid or minoxidil edema incidence within the search budget.
